transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-08-21 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Nimbus Head of MLOps), Carlos Mendez (Nimbus Platform Eng), Avery Thompson (Nimbus SRE)

Summary (auto):
- Follow-up on customer escalation after 2025-08-19 incident where intermittent GPU OOMs led to partial fallbacks to CPU and sustained latency SLO breaches during peak traffic windows.
- Reviewed timeline, immediate mitigations, proposed long-term fixes and rollback/rollback guards.
- Agreed immediate canary with batch-size caps, model pin + quantized variant, and run microbenchmarks to validate dedicated pool capacity.
- Action items captured and next steps assigned.

Topics:
- Incident timeline & root-cause hypotheses
- Immediate mitigations (canary config, batch caps, KV cache hygiene)
- Dedicated pool sizing and fallback policies
- Runbook updates and customer-facing comms
- Security/PCI impact questions around KMS rotation and audit logs

Action items (recorded in call):
- Maya to share postmortem draft and annotated timeline (link) by 2025-08-22
- Liam to perform microbenchmarks and upload spreadsheet to shared drive by 2025-08-27
- Carlos to reproduce sequence that triggered OOM in staging and file ticket by 2025-08-24

References:
- Postmortem draft (internal): https://redwood.internal/docs/nimbus/postmortem-2025-08-19
- Runbook patch (proposed): https://redwood.internal/runbooks/kv-cache-and-oom
- Benchmark template: https://sheets.example.com/nimbus-microbenchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay, hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh it's Maya from Redwood — we're here to run through the escalation follow up and the mitigation roadmap. we have about 45 minutes, does that still work?
[00:18] Priya Singh: yes that's fine, thanks. we got a lot of internal questions after the incident on monday, so this is timely.
[00:29] Liam O'Rourke: quick intro from me — liam, i'm the se on the account, i'll walk through the timeline and the suggested short-term mitigations.
[00:36] Carlos Mendez: quick note — we replayed the traces, we're seeing the OOMs cluster around long sequences and large batch requests at 12:30 in our region. some requests dropped to CPU fallback and caused a 3x latency spike.
[00:52] Avery Thompson: and to add, some of our tooling didn't pick up the degrade because the request sampler missed the higher tail. so alerting needs tuning.
[01:06] Maya Chen: okay, let's step through the timeline — liam, you captured the snapshot?
[01:12] Liam O'Rourke: yeah, so timeline from our side — at 12:27 we saw a surge in concurrent streams, roughly 2.5x baseline. at 12:29 a few GPU pods reported memory pressure and the runtime triggered CPU fallback for three pods, the system's fallback path increased per-token latency by ~250ms on average, and because the KV cache (the K-V cash on some transcripts) had fragmented entries we saw cache miss amplification — so more work hit the model.
[01:42] Priya Singh: can i ask — is the kv cache fragmentation a redwood thing or a pattern from our client behavior?
[01:49] Liam O'Rourke: it's a little of both; the runtime has a GC window for prefix cache and when you have unusual sequence length variation, entries don't get reused as much. combined with bursty batching it amplifies memory usage.
[02:04] Carlos Mendez: we did also run a custom prompt with 12k tokens which i know is higher than typical — that looked like the initial trigger.
[02:12] Maya Chen: important to call out — the customer-facing SLA was breached for ~18 minutes during the peak. that's the immediate escalation cause.
[02:21] Priya Singh: yep, that was what got our ops folks up. we need a stop-gap that prevents a repeat while we do deeper changes.
[02:30] Liam O'Rourke: for stop-gap, recommended stack: 1) conservative canary: pin to quantized model variant for the canary traffic, 2) enforce batch size caps at the gateway, 3) KV cache bypass for very long sequences so they don't fragment hot cache, 4) set autoscale conservative thresholds so we don't rely on instantaneous scaling.
[02:52] Avery Thompson: can you expand on 'KV cache bypass'? what would that look like operationally?
[02:57] Liam O'Rourke: basically tag the request with a header when sequence > X and route to a pool that disables prefix caching — that reduces cache fragmentation but increases per-token compute; the idea is to isolate the long sequence cost.
[03:13] Priya Singh: does that increase cost dramatically? we have to balance SLOs and cost.
[03:18] Maya Chen: yes it can — that's why the canary is to measure real effect. also a suggestion is to route long sequences to dedicated capacity rather than hosted pool.
[03:28] Carlos Mendez: we are interested in dedicated pool if it avoids noisy neighbor effects. what sizing do you recommend for our traffic profile?
[03:36] Liam O'Rourke: initial recommended headroom: a 1.5x buffer on top of peak observed tokens/sec and a small burst reserve; we'll run microbenchmarks to create a tailored sizing guidance.
[03:46] Priya Singh: timeline for benchmarks?
[03:49] Liam O'Rourke: we can run a 4-hour window on your staging next week, upload the sheet with seq length buckets. aiming for results by 2025-08-27.
[03:59] Maya Chen: on the runbook updates, we proposed adding playbook steps: immediate rollback, escalate to SE/engineers, toggle canary, and onscreen communication to customers. link posted in chat.
[04:12] Avery Thompson: alerting — we need a better tail-sampling and a synthetic that hits the long sequence path.
[04:19] Carlos Mendez: agreed, we will add a synthetic aligned to the 12k token request and tie an SLO alert at p99 + p999.
[04:28] Priya Singh: question on security — we saw a KMS key rotation last month, could that interplay cause additional latencies and contributed to the window?
[04:35] Liam O'Rourke: unlikely to be the primary cause — KMS latencies would add small ms to setup steps, but we can validate. we'll run a latency profile with KMS calls on the critical path.
[04:45] Maya Chen: action: carlos to open a ticket to validate KMS rotation impact by 2025-08-24.
[04:51] Carlos Mendez: will do.
[04:53] Priya Singh: for customer comms, we want a short summary and a promise of timeline for mitigation.
[04:59] Maya Chen: we'll prepare a 2-paragraph public-safe summary + internal technical appendix. maya to share by 2025-08-22.
[05:06] Liam O'Rourke: technical deep-dive — discussing long-term fixes: better memory-aware scheduling in runtime, kernel selection improvements so the model's per-token memory profile is lower, and implementing smarter KV eviction (LRU variants tuned to seq distribution).
[05:22] Priya Singh: those sound good but long lead; do you have estimates?
[05:26] Liam O'Rourke: rough: memory-aware scheduling and kernel improvements are 6–8 weeks; KV eviction tweaks could be 2–3 weeks with a canary. we can backport some conservative patches faster.
[05:38] Avery Thompson: can we get a prioritized list and owners so we know what to expect?
[05:43] Maya Chen: yes — we'll capture a roadmap: 1) stop-gap canary & batch caps (this week), 2) run microbenchmarks & sizing (next week), 3) runbook + alerting updates (this week), 4) medium-term runtime patches (4–8 weeks).
[05:58] Carlos Mendez: any compliance impact from enabling KV cache bypass or moving to dedicated pools? encryption in flight/stored?
[06:05] Liam O'Rourke: dedicated pools maintain same encryption at rest and in transit; KMS integrations unchanged. bypassing prefix caching doesn't change persisted data — it's an in-memory runtime behavior. we'll share a short note for your security team.
[06:20] Priya Singh: perfect. also, competitors question — we did some benchmarking vs VendorX last quarter — their system fell over at similar load but recovered different ways; curious if Redwood's fallback was expected.
[06:31] Maya Chen: different runtimes have different fallback semantics. ours prefers correctness (complete response) over dropping requests, so CPU fallback is intentional; we need to tune when that happens.
[06:42] Priya Singh: okay, that explains it.
[06:46] Liam O'Rourke: last thing — instrumentation. we'll add a new metric: oom_fallback_count and kv_miss_amplification_ratio so we can correlate.
[06:58] Carlos Mendez: please add tags to metrics so our dashboards can pull them.
[07:02] Maya Chen: noted.
[07:04] (brief silence, typing)
[07:18] Priya Singh: recap from our side: we want the canary this week, microbenchmarks next week, postmortem to customers by 2025-08-24 if possible.
[07:28] Maya Chen: we'll aim for that cadence — maya to share the internal postmortem draft + public-safe summary by 2025-08-22, liam will orchestrate the benchmark plan, carlos will run staging repro and validate KMS.
[07:40] Avery Thompson: okay, any risks to starting the canary? any chance it could replicate the outage?
[07:46] Liam O'Rourke: the canary is conservative — pinned quantized variant + batch cap should reduce peak memory. risk low; still monitoring window will be 48 hours.
[07:55] Priya Singh: sounds reasonable.
[07:58] Maya Chen: all right, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark window and upload the postmortem.
[08:06] Carlos Mendez: thanks, talk soon.
[08:09] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcription quality: a few terms were auto-corrected ("KV cache" appears as "K-V cash" in some auto-transcripts), proper nouns may be inconsistent. The recording had occasional speaker-attribution confusion during crosstalk.
